summary: Adds a sentence to the Very Distant Host specification in Appendix F of BBN Report 1822: null packets do not use a channel or channel number when sent and are not acknowledged when received.

plainLanguage.summary: A rulebook was missing one sentence, so this note adds it: empty filler messages do not need a lane or a reply.

subtitle: A clarification to the early network host-IMP interface specification.

tldr.problem: The Very Distant Host specification in BBN Report 1822 was missing a detail about null packets and how they should be handled.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a single clarifying sentence: null packets do not use a channel or channel number when sent, and are not acknowledged when received.
tldr.outcome: This clarification helped implementers understand the protocol correctly without needing to wait for a full revision of the specification.

today: RFC 591 is an informal clarification to an earlier specification document.

sections.title: The Missing Clarification
sections.content:
RFC 591 is a brief note that adds a clarifying sentence to the Very Distant Host specification found in Appendix F of BBN Report 1822, which describes how a host computer connects to an IMP (Interface Message Processor) in the early ARPANET.

The specification was incomplete regarding the handling of null packets—messages with no data payload—and this ambiguity needed to be cleared up for implementers building compatible systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer interface rulebook forgot to say how to send empty messages. This note says: send them without a numbered slot and do not wait for confirmation.

sections.title: Null Packets in the Protocol
sections.content:
In the host-IMP interface, null packets are messages that contain no actual data. The clarification states that null packets do not use a channel (nor a channel number) when sent and are not acknowledged when received. This means the sender does not need to wait for an acknowledgment after sending a null packet.

This rule distinguishes null packets from regular data packets, which follow normal channel allocation and acknowledgment rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Empty messages are simple: they skip the fancy routing system and do not expect a reply. That makes them quick and easy to handle.

sections.title: Context and Status
sections.content: This RFC was published in November 1973 as an addendum to the BBN Report 1822 specification, which was a key document for building ARPANET hosts and IMPs. The author, D. Walden from BBN, noted that readers of the specification should file this RFC with their copy of the report until the report itself was updated to include the clarification.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a quick fix to an important rulebook before the rulebook could be officially reprinted with the missing sentence included.
